Yesterday you ran `pd.read_csv()` and a DataFrame appeared. Today you slow that line down
and learn what it actually does, what it gives you back, and how to steer it. Everything
this week starts with getting data into Python correctly, so this is the most load-bearing
hour of the course.

By the end of this session you will be able to:

- read a CSV from a URL or a file path into a DataFrame
- explain the difference between a **DataFrame** and a **Series**
- choose a column to serve as the **index**
- get the column names out as a Python **list**, and use a list to select columns

## Importing pandas

Every notebook that touches data starts the same way:

```{python}
import pandas as pd
```

`import pandas` makes the library available. `as pd` gives it a short nickname so you can
write `pd.read_csv()` instead of `pandas.read_csv()`. Essentially every pandas user on
earth writes `pd`, so we will too.

## Our data for today

We'll work with air quality measurements from an OpenAQ monitoring station in Goleta,
just up the road from Bren.

```{python}
url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/openaq_goleta_measurments.csv'
```

Notice we put the address in a **variable** first. This is a habit worth forming: the URL
is long, you'll use it more than once, and naming it keeps your `read_csv` line readable.

## `pd.read_csv()`

Here is the whole sentence:

```{python}
goleta = pd.read_csv(url)
```

That's it. `pd.read_csv()` takes a location, goes and gets the file, parses the commas, and
hands you back a **DataFrame**. Let's look at the first few rows:

```{python}
goleta.head()
```

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 `read_csv` is happy with either a web address or a path to a file on disk. These two
are the same idea:

```python
df = pd.read_csv('https://example.org/data.csv')   # from the web
df = pd.read_csv('data/measurements.csv')          # from a folder next to your notebook
```

This week we mostly read from the web, because then everyone in the room has exactly the
same file.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
The Santa Barbara station's data is at the same address, but with
`openaq_santa_barbara_measurments.csv` on the end. Read it into a variable called
`santa_barbara` and display its first few rows.
:::

## DataFrames and Series

A **DataFrame** is a table: rows and named columns, like a well-behaved spreadsheet.

Pull a single column out and you get a **Series**, which is one column of values with the
row labels still attached:

```{python}
goleta['value']
```

Check the types to see the difference plainly:

```{python}
print(type(goleta))
print(type(goleta['value']))
```

This distinction matters more than it looks. Many pandas methods return a Series, and
knowing you're holding one column rather than a table tells you what you can do next.

```{python}
goleta['value'].head()
```

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 Square brackets with **one column name** give you a Series. Square brackets with a
**list of column names** give you back a DataFrame, even if the list has one item:

```python
goleta['value']       # Series
goleta[['value']]     # DataFrame with one column
```
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Pull out the `parameter` column. Confirm with `type()` that you have a Series, then display
its first five values.
:::

## Column names as a list

You often want to know what's in a table before you do anything else. The `.columns`
attribute tells you:

```{python}
goleta.columns
```

That's a pandas object. To get a plain Python **list**, which is easier to read and to work
with, use `.tolist()`:

```{python}
column_names = goleta.columns.tolist()
column_names
```

A **list** is Python's basic container for an ordered collection of things. You write one
with square brackets and commas:

```{python}
parameters_we_care_about = ['o3', 'pm25']
parameters_we_care_about
```

You get items out by **position**, counting from zero:

```{python}
print(column_names[0])
print(column_names[1])
```

And `len()` tells you how many items there are:

```{python}
len(column_names)
```

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 Counting from zero trips up everyone at first. The first item is at position `0`, the
second at `1`, and the last one is at `len(x) - 1`. You can also count backwards: `[-1]` is
the last item.
:::

```{python}
column_names[-1]
```

## Selecting columns with a list

Here's where the list pays off. Hand `read_csv`'s result a list of column names and you get
a smaller DataFrame with just those columns:

```{python}
keep = ['location_name', 'parameter', 'value', 'unit']
goleta[keep].head()
```

You'll see this written both ways. The inner brackets are the list, the outer brackets are
the selection:

```{python}
goleta[['location_name', 'parameter', 'value', 'unit']].head()
```

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Build a list called `time_columns` containing `'datetimeUtc'` and `'datetimeLocal'`, then
use it to display just those two columns from `goleta`.
:::

## Choosing the index with `index_col=`

Every DataFrame has an **index**: the labels down the left-hand side. By default pandas
numbers the rows `0, 1, 2, ...`. You saw those numbers in `head()`.

Sometimes a column in the file is a better label than a row number. `index_col=` tells
`read_csv` to use one:

```{python}
goleta_by_time = pd.read_csv(url, index_col='datetimeLocal')
goleta_by_time.head()
```

The local timestamp is now the row label, and it's no longer one of the columns:

```{python}
goleta_by_time.columns.tolist()
```

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 `index_col=` is our first **keyword argument**: an argument you pass by name rather than
by position. `read_csv` has dozens of them, and you'll meet a few more this week. The
pattern is always `name=value`, after the required arguments.
:::

:::{.callout-caution title="Choosing an index"}
An index is most useful when its values are meaningful and unique. `location_name` would be
a poor choice here, since every row has the same station name. A timestamp is a good choice,
because it identifies the row.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Read the Goleta file again, this time using `datetimeUtc` as the index, into a variable
called `goleta_utc`. How many columns does it have compared to the original `goleta`?
:::

## Putting it together

You now have the first sentence of every workflow you'll write:

```python
import pandas as pd

url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/some_file.csv'
df = pd.read_csv(url)
df.head()
```

## Key points

- `import pandas as pd` once, at the top of every notebook.
- `pd.read_csv(location)` reads a CSV from a URL or a file path and returns a **DataFrame**.
- `df['col']` gives a **Series** (one column). `df[['a', 'b']]` gives a **DataFrame**.
- `df.columns.tolist()` gives you the column names as a plain Python **list**.
- Lists are ordered, written with `[]`, indexed from `0`, and measured with `len()`.
- `index_col='name'` chooses which column becomes the row labels.
